commitResults.messageTitle: Rename main class and added a greeting
Add support for echo
Add support for list and bye
Code refactor: added LogBook and Task extensions
Updated LogBook class to utilise an ArrayList instead of Array
Added mark and unmark task features
Created the ToDo, Deadline and Event classes
Added support for tracking ToDo, Deadlines and Events
Error handling with exceptions
Added support for deleting tasks from the list
Add Command enum to represent supported commands
Improve Javadoc phrasing of the changeStatus method
Feat: load saved tasks from data file on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Task live only in memory, so the list starts empty on every run and
anything recorded in a previous session is lost.

Persisting the list lets a user close Hermes and pick up where they left
off.

Let's
* add a Task constructor accepting the completion status, so a stored
  task is rebuilt in the state it was saved in rather than created
* give each task type a fileContent() method returning its
  pipe-delimited text form and widen Task's fields to protected so
  subclasses can read them
* have LogBook read data/Hermes.txt when constructed, dispatching on the
  type letter to rebuild the matching task

Current Hermes.txt file is hardcoded, system supports read functionality
only.

commitResults.messageTitle: Feat: Persists task changes to the data file
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are read from data/Hermes.txt on startup, but changes made during
a session are never written back to be saved for the next session.

Upon making any changes to the logBook ArrayList in LogBook class,
immediately save the updated state to the Hemes.txt file.

Let's,
* add LogBook.save(), writing the whole in-memory list to the file
* call it from log(), mark(), unmark() and delete()
* declare fileContent() abstract on Task, so every task type is
  obliged to define how it is stored

Rewriting the file in full, rather than appending or patching a single
line, keeps the in-memory list as the only source of truth.

The full rewrite costs more I/O per command, which is not measurable at
this scale.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle data file errors without losing tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The storage layer assumes the data file exists and that every line
in it is well formed. A first run, a truncated line, an unrecognised
type letter, or a read-only file will each either crash Hermes or
discard a task without saying anything.

Let's,
* treat a missing file as a first run, creating the data directory
  and starting with an empty list
* require each line to have exactly the field count its type letter
  implies, no blank fields, and a completion flag of 0 or 1
* count the lines failing those checks and report the total at
  startup, naming the file so it can be repaired before the next save
* reject task fields containing '|', which would otherwise be written
  and then be unreadable on the next startup
* translate a failed write into a HermesException, so the session
  carries on with the change still held in memory

Unreadable lines are skipped rather than treated as fatal, which
keeps the remaining tasks usable, and the startup warning is what
stops that loss being silent. A failed write leaves the file intact
and the work in memory, so ending the session would destroy more
than it protects.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
tweak Deadline and Event to utilise LocalDateTime instead of String
Add a DateTimeFormat.java file to perform parsing
commitResults.messageBody:
Users will have their own unique way of typing their date time for
Deadline and Event.

The DateTimeFormat.java file explores many possible ways date time can
be written and selects the appropriate formatter to parse the string.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parse deadline and event times as LocalDateTime
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadlines and events stored their times as free-form strings, so
Hermes could not display them in a consistent format and had no way
to compare or sort by them later.

Separate the three roles a date format plays:

* Input accepts many patterns, since users type dates in many ways.
* Storage uses one fixed format, ISO-8601 via LocalDateTime's own
  toString and parse. It is machine-facing, so it can stay stable
  even if the display format changes.
* Display uses a single formatter shared by all tasks, held on Task
  as "dd MMM yyyy HHmm".

Guard task construction in the loader as well. A line can pass
isWellFormed, which only checks field count and emptiness, and still
carry a date that will not parse. Because LogBook is a static field
of Hermes, that exception previously escaped the constructor during
class initialisation and killed the program before the greeting,
taking every valid task with it. Counting the line as skipped
instead means one bad date costs one task, and the existing startup
warning reports it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a due command to list tasks that are due by a date
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks now carry real dates, but there was no way to ask which ones
are coming up — the user had to read through list and compare dates
by eye, which does not scale past a handful of tasks.

Add "due /by <date>", which reuses DateTimeFormat.parseTime for the
cutoff and returns the incomplete tasks falling on or before it,
soonest first. An empty result gets its own message rather than an
empty reply.

Give Task an abstract dueDateTime(): a deadline answers with its by
time, an event with its start, and a todo with null. Making it
abstract rather than giving Task a null-returning default means a
future task type cannot compile until it decides what its date is.
An earlier draft used an inherited default and Deadline silently
missed the override, so deadlines were absent from the one command
written for them.

Keep the query read-only. It sorts inside the stream rather than
sorting the backing list, so running due does not renumber the
entries the user sees in list, and delete 1 still means the same
task before and after.

Have Task implement Comparable in preparation for a sort command,
ordering active dated tasks before undated ones and completed tasks
last. Ranking the groups first and only then comparing dates keeps
the comparison antisymmetric and transitive; an ordering built from
a chain of early returns satisfies neither, and TimSort rejects such
comparators outright on longer lists.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add sort functionality to the system
commitResults.messageBody:
The task lists can get long and users lack a clear visibility of what
they should prioritise.

To improve the visibility and effectively utilise having deadlines and
event class fields stored as LocalDateTime, let's add a new sort command
to sort the list in accordance to their due date with tasks due soon
pushed to the top, enhancing visibility.

Sorting will update the order in which the list is stored in the LogBook
class and update the saved file in Hermes.txt.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
update AGENTS.md to reflect project state
Add text-UI regression tests and two project skills
commitResults.messageBody:
Refactoring the code into separate classes is about to move a lot of
behaviour between files. Doing that safely needs a way to confirm the
program still says exactly what it said before, which until now meant
running commands by hand and reading the output.

Add test/ui-test-plan.md, holding eleven cases that each record an aim,
optional starting contents for the data file, the commands to type and
the expected reply. Cases cover adding each task type, the accepted
date formats, mark, unmark, delete, due, sort, persistence across a
restart, recovery from unreadable storage lines, and rejection of bad
input.

Add test/run-ui-tests.py to execute the plan. It compiles the sources
fresh, runs each case in a throwaway working directory and compares the
output, stopping at the first failure. The throwaway directory matters:
LogBook opens data/Hermes.txt by a path relative to the working
directory, so running tests from the project root would overwrite the
user's real task list. A case may hold several input blocks, which run
as successive launches sharing one data directory, and that is what
makes the two restart cases possible.

Comparison skips the startup banner, the divider rules and blank lines,
so an expected block records what Hermes said rather than how the reply
was framed. Everything else must match exactly.

Add two project skills. test-ui runs the plan above and reports the
console session. present-changes-visually renders a commit range or the
working tree as a side-by-side HTML diff; it is adapted from the se-edu
skill of the same name, which ships as a Codex skill, with the paths
moved under .claude and the reference to a craft-commit-message skill
replaced by a pointer to the conventions in AGENTS.md.

Stop tracking the Python bytecode cache, which was committed by
accident, and ignore it from now on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract console input and output into a Ui class
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes had grown to hold three unrelated responsibilities: talking to
the console, making sense of what the user typed, and deciding what to
do about it. This is the first of several steps splitting those apart,
starting with the console because it is the cleanest seam — the code
that prints a reply shares no data with the code that works out what
the reply should be.

Move the banner, the divider rules, the reply framing and the input
Scanner into Ui. It exposes showWelcome, hasNextCommand, readCommand,
show and showError. Hermes now works purely in strings and no longer
calls System.out at all, so how a reply is framed can change in one
place without touching any code that decides what to say. showError
currently just delegates to show; it exists so a caller can say which
of the two it means, and so error presentation can diverge later
without hunting through call sites.

Ui is an instance rather than a static utility, held in a static field
for now, since later steps will assemble Ui, Storage and the task list
in a constructor and this avoids changing its shape twice.

This step is behaviour-preserving. Feeding an identical script to the
program before and after produces byte-identical output, blank lines
and dividers included, and the same data file. All eleven cases in
test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move the messages Hermes authors into Ui
commitResults.messageBody:
The previous step routed every reply through Ui, but three pieces of
text were still written by Hermes itself: the goodbye in the bye case,
the unrecognised-command message in the unknown case, and the whole
skipped-lines warning. Those were the only strings Hermes composed
rather than forwarded, which made them the last presentation decisions
left in the dispatch switch.

Add showGoodbye, showUnknownCommand and showLoadingError to Ui and call
those instead. The pluralisation in the warning, which chooses between
"line"/"lines" and "it"/"them", moves with the message it belongs to;
Hermes keeps only the decision of whether there is anything to report,
which is control flow rather than wording.

showLoadingError is named after the method in the reference design for
this refactor, so the eventual constructor that loads tasks and reports
a failure has the method it expects to call.

Hermes now contains no user-facing text at all. Every string it passes
to Ui comes back from LogBook or from a HermesException.

This step is behaviour-preserving. Feeding an identical script to the
program produces byte-identical output against the baseline captured
before the Ui extraction began, the singular form of the warning still
reads "1 line ... skipped it", and all eleven cases in
test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract file reading and writing into a Storage class
commitResults.messageBody:
LogBook held two unrelated jobs: the list of tasks, and the data file
that list is kept in. Roughly half the class was file handling — the
File field, the loader, the line-shape validation, the writer and the
count of unreadable lines — none of which the list operations needed to
know about.

Move all of it to Storage, which takes a file path and exposes load()
returning the stored tasks and save(tasks) writing them back. Storage
is now the only class that knows the file exists, what a stored line
looks like, or how a line becomes a Task. LogBook keeps only the list
and the operations on it: log, mark, unmark, delete, sort, listTaskDueBy
and the numbering used by list.

LogBook takes a Storage in its constructor, loads through it, and hands
the list back after every change. Persistence stays where it was rather
than moving up to the caller, so no command handler can forget to save.
The cost is that LogBook depends on Storage and cannot be built without
one; the alternative, making the caller save, spreads that duty across
every handler and makes omissions silent.

Call storage.save(this.logBook) at each site instead of keeping a
private save() wrapper of the same name. The wrapper would have read
identically to the method it replaced while doing something quite
different, and the delegation is worth seeing.

Storage also owns skippedLines, since how many lines failed to parse is
a fact about reading the file rather than about the task list. Hermes
now asks storage rather than logBook for it.

Ui.showLoadingError takes the path as an argument. It previously spelled
out data/Hermes.txt in the message text while Storage held the real
path, so the filename was recorded in two places with nothing keeping
them in step.

This step is behaviour-preserving. Feeding an identical script to the
program produces byte-identical output against the baseline captured
before this refactor began. A first run with no data directory still
creates the file, a write to an unwritable file still reports the
failure and carries on, and all eleven cases in test/ui-test-plan.md
pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Hermes one path to storage instead of two
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes held a Storage field only to ask it two questions at startup: how
many records failed to load, and where they are kept. LogBook held the
same Storage for its real work, so the file layer was reachable by two
routes while the message that needed it was a single line of output.

Ask logBook.getSkippedLines() instead. Storage still counts the skipped
records, since it is the class that reads the file; LogBook forwards the
number and computes nothing. The question reads correctly in LogBook's
own vocabulary — whether the task list holds everything that was saved —
so this is not the file layer leaking upward.

Have Hermes own the data path as a DATA_PATH constant rather than asking
for it. Hermes is where the parts are assembled, so knowing where data
lives is already its job, and Storage is now built inline and handed
straight to the only class that uses it. Storage.getPath existed solely
for the call this removes, so it goes too. Asking a task list for a
filesystem path would have been a genuine leak, unlike the skipped count.

Hermes now depends on Ui and LogBook alone.

The alternative was to follow the reference design literally, with
Hermes owning Storage and calling save itself after each change. That
removes the shared dependency but requires LogBook to hand out its
internal list, and restores the risk that a handler forgets to save.
Keeping persistence inside LogBook remains the better trade.

This step is behaviour-preserving. Feeding an identical script to the
program produces byte-identical output against the baseline captured
before this refactor began, and all eleven cases in
test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command interpretation into a Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes held about 150 lines of input handling: splitting arguments on
/by and /from, checking that the pieces were present, converting task
numbers, and building tasks. That left the main class knowing how every
command is worded, which is not the job of the class that runs the
conversation.

Move it to Parser, which turns text into the values the rest of Hermes
works with: a Command, a task number, a Task, a cutoff date. Hermes
shrinks from 245 lines to 75 and is now a loop, a dispatch switch and
three collaborators.

Have the task parsers return a Task rather than the pieces of one. The
obvious alternative, returning a description and a date for the caller
to assemble, needs a different return type per command and pushes the
knowledge of which fields make a Deadline back into Hermes. Building a
Task from text is making sense of the command, so it belongs here.

Separate the MARK and UNMARK cases, which previously shared a branch and
a helper that switched on which of the two it had been given. Each now
reads as one line.

Move the pipe separator and its check from Hermes to Storage. That a
field cannot contain '|' is a fact about the stored format, and Storage
is the only class that writes those lines. It is static because it
describes the format rather than any particular file, so Parser can
check text without holding a Storage.

This step is behaviour-preserving, including the parts that are merely
inconsistent. The wording of the missing-number complaint still differs
between delete and mark, and addEvent still parses its dates before
checking for a separator while addDeadline checks first. Both are worth
tidying, but not in a commit whose value is that nothing changed.

Feeding an identical script to the program produces byte-identical
output against the baseline captured before this refactor began. A
second run of 28 malformed inputs, covering every validation branch in
the moved code, is byte-identical against the previous commit. All
eleven cases in test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to Keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
The enum named Command does not represent a command so much as name
one: it pairs the word the user types with an example of correct usage,
and carries no ability to do anything. The next step introduces objects
that hold a parsed command and execute it, and Command is the right
name for those.

Rename the enum to Keyword, which is what it actually holds, and free
the name before anything depends on it. Rename fromKeyword to of, since
Keyword.fromKeyword reads as a stutter, and Keyword.of("todo") does not.

Settle two method names in Parser that the rename made ambiguous.
parseCommand returned a Keyword rather than a command, so it is now
parseKeyword; the method returning the raw first word, previously
parseKeyword, is now parseCommandWord. One returns the enum, the other
returns text, and neither name now suggests the other's job.

This commit is a rename and nothing else, kept separate so the change of
shape that follows is readable on its own.

Feeding an identical script to the program produces byte-identical
output against the baseline captured before this refactor began, 28
malformed inputs are byte-identical against the previous commit, and all
eleven cases in test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command switch with Command objects
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes decided what every command did. Its dispatch switch named all ten
of them and spelled out the calls each one made, so adding a command
meant editing the class that runs the conversation, and Hermes could not
be read without knowing the whole command set.

Introduce an abstract Command with execute(logBook, ui) and isExit, and
one subclass per command. Each holds its own already-parsed data — a
task, an index, a cutoff — and knows the single thing it does. Hermes
now runs whatever it is handed:

    Command command = parser.parse(input);
    command.execute(logBook, ui);
    isRunning = !command.isExit();

The main loop is down to 54 lines from 75, and no longer names a single
command.

Let Parser build the commands. Choosing which command was typed is
reading the input, so the switch belongs with the parsing rather than
with the running. Parser gained that switch and lost its public surface:
parse is now the only public method, and the seven parsing helpers are
private, since a command that comes back is already complete and callers
have no reason to assemble one themselves.

Use one AddCommand for todo, deadline and event. Parser already produces
the right kind of Task, so all three do identical work, and three
classes differing only in their constructor argument would be noise.

Make not recognising a command a Command of its own rather than a case
the loop handles. Ending the conversation likewise moved into isExit, so
the flag that exists because a switch cannot break out of a loop is now
just the answer to a question asked of the command.

This step is behaviour-preserving. Feeding an identical script to the
program produces byte-identical output against the baseline captured
before this refactor began, 28 malformed inputs covering every
validation branch are byte-identical against the previous commit, and
all eleven cases in test/ui-test-plan.md pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'A-MoreOOP'
Organise the classes into packages under hermes
commitResults.messageBody:
Twenty-two classes sat in the default package, so nothing about the
source tree said which of them dealt with the console, which with
storage, and which with parsing. That structure existed in the code
after the last few refactorings but was invisible in the file list.

Move them under a hermes root, keeping src/main/java as the source
folder:

  hermes/          Hermes, HermesException
  hermes/command/  Command and its nine subclasses
  hermes/parser/   Parser, Keyword, DateTimeFormat
  hermes/task/     Task, ToDo, Deadline, Event, LogBook, Storage
  hermes/ui/       Ui

Group Storage with the task classes rather than giving it a package of
its own. Splitting them would create a cycle, since LogBook holds a
Storage while Storage builds Tasks and it would also break LogBook's
access to Task's protected members, which is legitimate precisely
because the two belong together. Keeping them in one package makes
Storage an implementation detail of how tasks are kept, which nothing
outside needs to know. The cost is that persistence is no longer
visible in the package list; if a second kind of data ever needed
storing, Storage would move out then.

Put HermesException beside Hermes rather than in a package of its own.
It is thrown by the parser, by storage and by every command, so it is
shared vocabulary rather than a layer, and a package holding one class
earns little. This does mean the root package and its subpackages
reference each other, but a cycle through the package that holds the
entry point is expected of a composition root.

Keep Keyword and DateTimeFormat with Parser, which is the only class
that uses either.

No member needed widening for this. Everything crossing a new package
boundary was already public, and the only protected access is
LogBook's use of Task, which the layout keeps in one package.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
Point the UI test runner and README at the packaged layout
Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Update the file to reflect the hermes name
Add JUnit tests for the parser and the task list
commitResults.messageBody:
The only automated check so far was the text-UI suite, which drives the
whole program through stdin and compares printed output.

Add ParserTest, covering the five ways a command can name a task type
without supplying what that type needs.

Add LogBookTest, covering listTaskDueBy. That method is the only public
one on LogBook that does not write to storage.

Two of its eight cases record decisions rather than exercise lines. The
cutoff is inclusive, so a task due at exactly the moment asked about is
listed, which pins down !isAfter against isBefore.

Point the tests at a JUnit @TempDir rather than the real data file.
LogBook cannot be constructed without a Storage, and adding a task
writes through it, so without this the tests would overwrite the user's
own tasks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
Add JavaDoc comments to all non-trivial methods
Mandate the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no recorded coding standard, so style decisions are
made case by case and cannot be checked against anything.

Let's record the SE-EDU Java standard (intermediate level) as the
seedu-java-coding-standard skill, and require it in AGENTS.md for all
Java written here. The skill carries the naming, layout, import,
statement and Javadoc rules, plus the commands that catch the
mechanically checkable ones.

Its Javadoc rules are stricter than the existing guidance on comments,
which asks for them only on nontrivial methods. AGENTS.md says the
standard supersedes that rather than deleting it, so the older advice
is not silently contradicted.

Also repair the Code Updates list, which had no lead-in sentence and
numbered both its items 2.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mandate the SE-EDU Git conventions
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages here follow no recorded convention beyond a line in
AGENTS.md asking for enough detail to explain the rationale, so subject
form, length limits and body structure are left to judgement.

Let's record the SE-EDU Git conventions as the seedu-git-standard
skill, and require it in AGENTS.md for all commits and branches. The
skill carries the subject line rules, the body structure of present
situation, reason, action and rationale, the 72-character wrap, and
the branch naming format, along with the guide's worked examples.

The existing rationale line is folded into the new bullets, which say
the same thing more precisely. The lightweight tag rule and the
instruction not to commit unless asked are unchanged.

Branches named for course increments, such as branch-A-Packages, stay
as they are. A grader looking for that exact name is a stronger
constraint than the kebab-case convention.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
Several files break rules of the standard this project follows:
wildcard imports, a constant and a parameter named in the wrong case,
a collection with a singular name, an over-length line, and seventeen
public classes and methods with no header comment.

Let's fix each of those. Comments on Task and its subclasses stay to
one line, since the standard allows omitting @param and @return where
the names already explain themselves.

Behaviour is unchanged: output is byte-identical to the previous
commit, and all UI and JUnit tests pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'adopt-seedu-standards'
Add search functionality to find tasks based on a keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Users may have a long lists of tasks and require a search functionality
to narrow their view to a few relevant tasks.

Let's add a find feature to help users filter out their task list
* Add a findTask method in logbook to search through all the tasks and
  return only the tasks which contains the keyword in their task
  description.
* Add a parseFind method so as to help ensure that users are utilising
  the find command correctly, inputting exactly one keyword only.
* Add a new FIND keyword into the Keyword ENUM.
* Add a new FindCommand class to execute the find operation.

The find feature is case insensitive because users cannot be expected to
remember the exact case of the keywords.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
fix minor typos
Add Checkstyle to enforce coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard is recorded in AGENTS.md and a skill but AI may miss
out on coding standard violations.

To perform deterministic checks on concrete aspects of the coding
standards, let's add the Checkstyle plugin with a config covering the
standard's rule.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix the violations Checkstyle reports
commitResults.messageBody:
Checkstyle was added in the previous commit and fails on twelve
violations: non explicit imports (e.g. import .*), imports out of group
and alphabetical order, a static field declared after instance fields,
line wraps starting with an open parenthesis, and a missing newline
at end of file.

Let's fix each of those. They are formatting only and does not change
the program's behaviour.

The one remaining report, a switch with no default in Storage.java, is
suppressed by comment rather than fixed. Unrecognised type letters are
already filtered out before that switch, so a default clause there
would be unreachable.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CheckStyle'
Update dependencies to support Java FX
Add a JavaFX window alongside the console UI
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes only has a console interface, to make Hermes more user friendly,
a user interface is required.

Let's add the two classes JavaFX needs to open a window, showing a
placeholder label for now. Main holds the Application lifecycle, and
Launcher is the entry point Gradle runs.

Launcher exists because the JavaFX runtime will not start when the
main class extends Application and javafx.graphics is not on the
module path. A class that does not extend Application avoids that
check.

Main is kept apart from Hermes rather than having Hermes extend
Application, so the class that assembles the program stays free of
JavaFX and can still be built and tested without a toolkit. The
console interface is untouched, and is what the window will be wired
to in future updates.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a chat window with placeholder replies
commitResults.messageBody:
The window shows a placeholder label, so there is no way to type
anything or to see what Hermes would say back.

Let's build the chat interface: MainWindow lays out a scrolling
transcript, a text field and a send button, and DialogBox renders one
turn of the conversation as an avatar beside its text. User and Hermes
boxes use the same class, with the Hermes one mirrored so the two
speakers sit on opposite sides.

DialogBox loads its own FXML through fx:root rather than a controller,
so each box is a self-contained component that MainWindow can create
as many of as it needs.

Replies are a placeholder that echoes the input back. Wiring the
window to the parser and task list comes next, and keeping that
separate means the layout can be checked on its own first.

commitResults.messageTitle: Anchor the nodes and set limit to Window size
commitResults.messageBody:
As the window size scales up, the text field, send button and scroll
pane does not adjust accordingly.

As the window size scales down, the text fiels, send button and scroll
pane become unusable as information gets covered.

Let's
* Anchor the scroll pane
* Anchor the text field
* Anchor the send button
* Set the minimum height and width of the window

commitResults.messageTitle: Show real replies in the GUI window
commitResults.messageBody:
The window echoes the input back, and Hermes only talks through a
console Ui, so the two cannot be joined: commands print their reply and
return nothing for a caller to display.

Let's have execute return its reply as a String instead of printing it.
The console loop wraps the result in ui.show, and the window puts it in
a dialog box, so both interfaces share one path through the parser and
the task list. The goodbye and unknown-command wordings move into their
commands, which is the only thing this costs.

Make Hermes an object built with a data path rather than a class of
static fields, so the window can hold one and ask it for responses.

Wire the window up: Main hands the controller a Hermes after loading
the FXML, the greeting is added when the window is built, and any
warning about unreadable records is added once Hermes exists. That
split matters, as initialize runs during FXML loading, before the
controller has been given anything.

Typing bye now closes the window after a pause long enough to read the
reply.

The console interface still behaves exactly as before, with all eleven
UI test cases passing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Style the chat window and guard empty input
commitResults.messageBody:
The window works but is unstyled, its text field and button hold their
position by fixed coordinates rather than anchors, and pressing Send on
an empty box adds a blank pair of dialog boxes.

Let's add stylesheets for the window and the dialog boxes, give the
input row left and right anchors so it stretches with the window
instead of drifting, and pad the reply label. Hermes replies carry a
style class of their own so the two speakers can be told apart at a
glance.

Ignore input that is empty, so Send on an empty box does nothing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-10'
Support deleting several tasks at once
commitResults.messageBody:
Delete takes a single task number, so clearing out a few finished
tasks means running the command once per task, and the numbers shift
after each run.

Let's accept any number of task numbers. LogBook.delete takes them as
varargs, so a single number still works and existing callers are
unaffected.

Every number is checked before any task is removed. Checking as each
task goes would leave the list half changed when a later number turns
out to be invalid, and since the exception escapes before the save,
memory and the data file would then disagree until some unrelated
command wrote the file.

The numbers are sorted first, so they may be given in any order, and
repeats are dropped while parsing. Sorting ascending also makes the
index shift predictable: every task already removed sits at a lower
index, so subtracting the number removed so far gives the right
position.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop repeated task numbers from crashing delete
commitResults.messageBody:
Delete drops repeated task numbers while they are still text, so two
spellings of the same number survive as separate entries. Every number
is checked before anything is removed, and both pass, because at that
point they still name a task that exists.

The removals then run one after another, each compensating for the
tasks already gone. The second copy is compensated for a removal that
was really itself, so it reaches for a position below the start of the
list and the program stops with an IndexOutOfBoundsException, taking
the session and any unsaved reply with it.

Let's drop repeats after the numbers have been converted rather than
before. Two spellings that mean the same task become the same value
once converted, so the second one is discarded and never reaches the
removal loop.

The trim that preceded the comparison goes too. The arguments are
split on whitespace, so no piece can contain any.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover bulk delete in the text-UI test plan
commitResults.messageBody:
Delete gained the ability to remove several tasks at once, but the
plan still describes it as taking a single number. Nothing exercises
giving more than one, giving them out of order, or naming a task that
does not exist, so the fix for repeated numbers rests on a manual
check that no one will repeat.

Let's add cases for removing several tasks, for numbers given in any
order or repeated, and for a delete cancelled by one bad number. The
repeated-number case names the same task in two spellings, which is
the input that used to end the session.

Wording the reply around the count left the single-task case reading
"removed the task", which TC-04 has failed on since. Let's choose
between "this task" and "these tasks" instead, so the plural reads
naturally and the original singular is restored.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the methods left bare by the GUI work
commitResults.messageBody:
Two methods added while building the window carry no header comment,
and checkstyle has reported them as errors ever since. A build that is
expected to fail is a build nobody reads, so the next real violation
would go unnoticed among them.

Let's describe the Hermes constructor and the window's initialize, and
the two neighbouring public methods the standard also asks for, so the
check passes and a fresh failure means something again.

Where initialize does its work is not obvious from the code, so its
comment records that it runs before the back end is attached, which is
why the greeting is raised there and the load warning is not.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe delete as the bulk operation it is
commitResults.messageBody:
Delete removes any number of tasks, but the names and comments around
it still describe removing one. DeleteCommand is documented as taking
one task, and holds the numbers in a field named for a single index.
LogBook.delete says it deletes a task, describes its parameter as one
index, and takes an array where the command that calls it accepts
varargs.

A reader who trusts the comments has to read the loop to find out the
method does something else, which is the opposite of what a header
comment is for.

Let's name the plural things in the plural, and take the numbers as
varargs in LogBook too, so a single number still reads as delete(0)
and the two signatures agree.

The reason all the numbers are checked before any task is removed is
recorded there as well, since the diff shows the ordering but not what
goes wrong without it.

Marking, unmarking and finding gained their missing parameter, return
and exception tags while their comments were being read.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the data file path in one place
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes declares the path of the data file as a constant, then names
the same path again where the console version is started and once
more where the window is. The constant ends up used only in the
message that reports an unreadable file.

Three copies of a path that must agree is a change waiting to go
wrong: pointing the constant somewhere else would move the warning
without moving the file, and the console and the window could as
easily drift apart from each other.

Let's add a constructor that takes no path and uses the constant, and
have both entry points call it. The constructor that names a file
stays, because that is what lets a test read a scratch file instead
of the list the user is really keeping.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the window ask whether the conversation ended
commitResults.messageBody:
The window decides when to close by testing whether the user typed the
word "bye". Command.isExit already answers that question, and the
console version asks it, but the reply reaching the window is a string
with nothing else in it.

Recognising the word a second time puts part of the command vocabulary
outside the parser, and the two copies do not agree: "BYE" is not a
command the parser knows, so the window reports it as unfamiliar and
then closes anyway. Adding a command that also ends the conversation
would need this test widened by hand.

Let's return the reply together with the answer isExit already gives,
as a small Response record, and have the window act on that. The
window keeps no opinion about which words end a conversation.

Empty input is now turned away before it is parsed rather than after,
and input is trimmed as the console version already trims it, so
stray spaces are not reported as an unfamiliar command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ui: separate composing a message from showing it
commitResults.messageBody:
showLoadingError prints the warning about unreadable records and also
returns it. The console version relies on the printing and throws the
return away; the window relies on the return and cannot stop the
printing, so starting the window on a damaged file writes the warning
to a console nobody is watching as well as into the dialogue.

A method named for showing something that quietly hands the caller a
copy is a seam left over from there being only one place to show
things.

Let's have it compose the warning and nothing else, under a name that
says so, and leave both callers to show the result where it belongs.

Making it static follows rejectSeparator in Storage: the wording
describes the situation rather than any one way of displaying it. That
in turn lets Hermes drop its Ui field, so the window no longer opens a
Scanner on console input it will never read.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tidy up small blemishes across the code
commitResults.messageBody:
A handful of small things have accumulated that each cost a reader a
moment. None of them is worth a commit alone, and together they are
easier to review as one.

Let's,
* reach for a task's completion and description through methods, so
  the fields stay the business of Task rather than of LogBook
* close the scanner with try-with-resources, so a line that throws
  while loading does not leak it
* drop the SuppressWarnings on load, which needs a checkstyle module
  the project does not enable and so suppresses nothing; the comment
  filter beside it is what actually works
* say why the FileNotFoundException below it cannot be reached
* return the reply from unmark directly, as mark already does
* hold the greeting as a constant and the window's images as final
* fix "at lease one keyword"

Nothing here changes what the program prints, apart from the spelling.

commitResults.messageTitle: LogBook: call a position an index, not an id
commitResults.messageBody:
LogBook names the task position it is given an id, while the commands
that supply it call the same value an index. Mark and unmark pass
index, delete passes indexes, and all three arrive as id.

An id suggests something that identifies a task for as long as it
exists. This value does not: it is a position, and every position
after a removed task shifts down. Reasoning about that shift is what
the bulk delete had to get right, and a name implying the numbers are
stable works against the reader.

Let's use index throughout, matching the callers and the checkIndex
helper that was already named for what it checks.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name methods returning many tasks in the plural
commitResults.messageBody:
listTaskDueBy and findTask each gather every task that matches and
return them together, but both are named as though they deal with one.

Singular and plural names are how a reader tells at a glance whether
they are getting one thing or a collection, and these two spend that
signal on the wrong answer.

Let's rename them listTasksDueBy and findTasks, and rename the test
methods that are named after the feature they exercise.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the remaining names that do not describe
commitResults.messageBody:
A scattering of names across the code say less than they could, or
say the wrong thing outright. Each is small, but together they make a
reader check the code to learn what a name should have told them.

Let's,
* call a task's text its description, the word the parser's own error
  messages already use, rather than a message
* give Deadline the noun its accessor already uses, dueDateTime, in
  place of the preposition by, matching start and end on Event
* rename parseFind to parseFindKeyword, since the parse methods
  beside it return the type they name and there is no Find type
* rename parseTime to parseDateTime, which is what it returns, and
  getFormat to findMatchingFormat, no longer a near-homophone of the
  getFormatter it sits above
* name the date patterns after their shape instead of DateFormatA
  through DateTimeFormatN, which were told apart only by a trailing
  letter, and case them as the constants they are
* rename warnAboutSkippedLines to describeSkippedLines, as it now
  composes the warning and leaves the showing to its caller
* spell out img, tmp and db, and call the Keyword a keyword in the
  parser helpers as the rest of the class already does

Nothing about the program's behaviour changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'naming-cleanup'
Add period to the end of all JavaDoc parameter description
Change method names from nouns to verbs
commitResults.messageBody:
To enhance code readability and alin with Java coding standards, let's
* Change the method name from fileContent to getFileContent()
* Change the method name from dueDateTime to getDueDateTime()

As these methods fundamentally performs the actions of extracting data,
organising them and returning it, phrasing them as a verb will make it
easier to understand what is happening when the methods get implemented.

commitResults.messageTitle: Update constructor parameter type from Boolean to boolean
Build the lines to be saved in Hermes.txt with a stream
commitResults.messageBody:
Saving creates an empty list, walks the tasks appending one formatted
line each, then writes the result.

Let's map the tasks to their file lines directly. The transformation
is then stated rather than assembled, and there is no mutable list to
follow between the declaration and the write.

commitResults.messageTitle: Raise the code quality of the task and parser code
commitResults.messageBody:
Several small things across the task and parser code make a reader
work harder than the logic warrants.

Marking and unmarking wrap the whole operation in an if-else, so the
ordinary case is nested and the reader meets the exceptional one
first. The sort ranks are bare numbers, leaving 0, 1 and 2 to be
decoded from the comparison that uses them. Local names such as parts
and due say less than they could, and several methods carry no header
comment at all.

Let's,
* return early when a task is already in the state asked for, so the
  work each method actually does is the un-nested path
* name the sort ranks with a TaskOrder enum, so the ordering is
  stated rather than implied by the numbers
* rename parts to argumentParts and due to dueDateTime, and pull the
  command word into a named local
* document the constructors and methods that were left bare
* settle on American spelling, as the coding standard asks

The enum orders its constants from soonest to last, so comparing them
by declaration order reproduces the ranking the numbers encoded, and
no comparison logic changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Task: tidy up after the sort rank refactor
commitResults.messageBody:
Replacing the numeric sort ranks with an enum left three things
behind. The constants are named in camel case where the standard asks
for screaming snake case, and checkstyle has no rule covering enum
constants, so the build never said so. The comment above getSortRank
is outdated and  explains the ranks as 0, 1 and 2, describing the very numbers
the enum removed. Rewriting mark as a guard clause dropped the full
stop from its reply, leaving it worded unlike the matching reply in
unmark.

Let's case the constants as constants, say what getSortRank returns
instead of what it used to return, and put the full stop back.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: extract reading one stored line
commitResults.messageBody:
Loading does three jobs at once. It decides whether the data file
exists and opens it, it walks the lines and counts the ones it cannot
use, and it decodes each line into the right kind of task. The method
was too long, deeply nested and difficult to read.

Let's move the decoding of a single line of information from storage to
parseStoredTask, constructing a Task object from the string. It will
return null if an invalid String was passed into the method. The load
method will still handle the core logic of reading the data from storage
and saving the Task objects created in the tasks ArrayList.

parseStoredTask will also return null as a default.

commitResults.messageTitle: Describe the stored task format in one enum
commitResults.messageBody:
The letter that identifies a kind of task in the data file is written
in five places. Each of the three kinds spells its own letter out when
formatting its line, and reading a line back switches on the letter
twice: once to learn how many fields the line should hold, and again
to build the task.

Nothing ties those places together, though the letter and the field
count are the same fact about the format. Adding a kind of task means
finding all five, and a count that disagreed with the line it
describes would surface only as records quietly skipped at load.

Let's name the kinds in a TaskType enum that holds the letter beside
the number of fields, and have both the writing and the reading ask it
rather than repeat it.

Looking the kind up before the fields are counted removes the first
switch outright. The second now switches over an enum rather than a
string, so it covers every case by construction, and the default that
stood in for an unrecognised letter goes as unreachable.

The letters themselves are unchanged, so files written by earlier
versions still load.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage: renamed parameter name from expectedFields to fieldCount
Assert the invariants that hold the code together
commitResults.messageBody:
Three places rely on a guarantee made somewhere else, and none of them
says so.

* Task.compareTo uses both due dates without checking for null. That is
safe because rank zero means the task has a date, but that rule lives
in sortRank, not here.
*LogBook.delete adjusts each position as it removes tasks. checkIndex
never sees the adjusted number. It stays in range only because the
parser sorted the numbers and dropped the repeats.
* Storage reads up to the fifth field of a stored line. That is safe
only because isWellFormed counted the fields first.

Let's assert each one where it is relied upon. These are not input
checks, so they stay assertions rather than exceptions: bad user input
is already refused, and anything that could make one of these false is
a fault in Hermes itself.

Assertions are off unless the runtime is asked for them, so let's turn
them on for the run task as well, or the checks would never execute
outside the tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Assertions into Master
commitResults.messageBody: Add assert statements to ensure key invariants that ensure the functionality of the code are ensured.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into branch-A-CodeQuality
commitResults.messageBody:
Resolve merge conflicts arising from:
* Task: The addition of the assert in master conflicted with the
strucutre in branch-A-CodeQuality. Let's restructure the code
to accomodate for both updates.
* Storage: The addition of the assert in master conflicted with
extract method refactor of the load method in branch-A-CodeQuality.
Follow the branch-A-CodeQuality structure and shift the assert line
to the parseStoredTask method.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into branch-A-Streams
Merge branch-A-CodeQuality into master
commitResults.messageBody: Improve the readability of the code.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Streams into master
Support marking and unmarking several tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Mark and unmark take a single task number, so changing the state of
multiple tasks will involve repeating the same command many times.

Let's accept any number of task numbers. Every number is checked
before any task is changed, so one bad number cancels the whole
command instead of leaving some tasks changed and unsaved.

Tasks already in the requested state are listed separately, so the
reply shows which of the given numbers has their state changed and
which tasks were alredy in the intended state.

Task.mark and Task.unmark now return whether they changed anything
rather than a sentence, which is what lets LogBook report on several
tasks at once.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix a potential NPE present in Storage.parseStoredTask method
commitResults.messageBody:
taskType.getStoredFieldCount() was called prior to checking if
taskType is a null value. This would lead to a NPE, hence the
method call was shifted to be only called after the null check.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an undo command
commitResults.messageBody:
There is no way back from a change. A delete aimed at the wrong task
number, or a mark meant for a different task, has to be put right by
hand, and a deleted task must be typed out again from memory.

Let's have LogBook keep the state of the list before each change and
add an undo command that restores the most recent one.

The saved state holds its own copy of every task rather than the tasks
themselves. Tasks are mutable: marking one sets a field on the object
in place, so a list holding the same objects would appear to change
along with the live list, and undoing a mark would restore a state
that had already been altered.

Each task copies itself through Task.copy, so LogBook does not need to
know whether it is holding a todo, a deadline or an event. This enables
deep copying of the tasks ArrayList to be stored in the cachedTask
stack.

A state is saved only once a command is certain to change something,
after the task numbers are checked and after any early return, so undo
never claims to reverse a command that did nothing.

Undo reaches back only over the current session, since the saved
states are held in memory rather than written to the data file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Restyle the chat window for easier reading
commitResults.messageBody:
The chat window keeps the look of the JavaFX tutorial it started from:
bright cyan bubbles with thick orange borders, square pictures and a
plain Send button. The strong colours and borders compete with the
text, and the two speakers' bubbles differ only in which corner is
squared off, so a conversation is harder to follow than it should be.

The window exists to hold a conversation, so the messages should stand
out and the decoration around them should recede. A cleaner layout is
easier for users to read and to find their way around.

Let's give the window a calmer chat style:
* light green bubbles for the user and white ones for Hermes, on a
  soft blue-grey background, with a faint shadow instead of a border
* a rounded input box and a rounded blue Send button with a
  paper-plane icon, so the place to type and send is obvious
* pictures cropped to circles with a thin grey border
* slim, translucent scroll bars that stay out of the way

Bubble text sets a font size but no family. With "Helvetica Neue",
JavaFX made wrapped bubbles one line too short and cut off their last
line, so the system font is used throughout instead.

Pictures are cropped from their centre rather than stretched to fill
the circle, so a photo that is not square keeps its proportions.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Shrink the profile pictures in the chat window
commitResults.messageBody:
The profile pictures are 99px across, several lines of text tall, so
they pull the eye away from the messages beside them.

Users come to the window to read the conversation, so the pictures
should only mark who is speaking and otherwise stay out of the way.

Let's shrink them to 40px across. At that size both pictures are still
easy to recognise, whereas a smaller circle made the photo hard to make
out and left the grey border taking up much of it.

The size is set through the circle's radius rather than by scaling it
in CSS. Scaling shrinks only how the circle is drawn and still reserves
the full 99px beside each bubble, so the text would not move over.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show error replies in red in the chat window
commitResults.messageBody:
Every reply from Hermes appears in the same white bubble, whether it
confirms what the user asked for or explains why it could not be done.
A refused command looks like a successful one until the user reads the
wording closely.

Showing problems in a different colour lets users see at a glance that
something went wrong and that the command needs another try.

Let's carry whether a reply reports a problem back in Response, beside
the text and the exit flag, and have the window show those replies in
a red bubble. A reply counts as an error when running the command
threw a HermesException.

The flag travels with the reply rather than being worked out from its
wording in the window, which would break the first time a message was
reworded.

The .error-label rule must stay after .reply-label in the stylesheet.
An error bubble carries both classes, and when two selectors are
equally specific the later rule decides the colour.

An unrecognised command is not an exception, so its reply stays white.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-BetterGUI'
Fix three replies that mislead or say nothing
commitResults.messageBody:
Three of Hermes's replies let the user down.

Adding a todo, deadline or event without a description calls the
missing part a "taskDescription", a variable name that leaked into the
wording during an earlier rename.

Entering a date Hermes cannot read suggests the format dd MM yyyy HHmm,
which Hermes rejects too, so following the advice only repeats the
error.

Listing an empty list prints nothing at all, leaving a new user with
no hint of what to do next.

Let's,
* say "description" in those replies
* suggest a date written the way Hermes reads it, 27 Aug 2026 1500
* have list explain how to add a first task when there are none

The empty-list hint lives in a new LogBook.listTasks rather than in
toString, because toString also builds the sort and undo replies,
which should keep showing the bare list.

Three ParserTest cases and text-UI case TC-07 still expect the old
wording and now fail. They are left for a later change that brings the
tests up to date.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the opening greeting in one place
commitResults.messageBody:
The greeting that opens a conversation is written out twice: once in
the console banner in Ui, and again as a constant in MainWindow for the
window. Changing what Hermes says first means finding and editing both,
and nothing stops the two copies from drifting apart.

Let's hold the greeting once, as Ui.GREETING, and have both the console
banner and the window read it from there.

The banner's wordmark moves into a constant of its own, so the greeting
can sit between it and the closing divider without being repeated. The
console prints exactly what it did before.

The window now shows the greeting across two lines, as the console
always has, instead of running both sentences together on one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Hermes a voice of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
Hermes replies like a generic assistant, with "Got it", "Roger",
"Sorry" and "Apologies", and nothing in its wording suggests who is
answering.

The chatbot is named after Hermes, messenger of the Olympian gods, and
its replies are the only place users meet that character. A consistent
voice makes the conversation more memorable without making it harder
to follow.

Let's reword every reply in a formal tone with a light touch of
Shakespearean English, and let some of them nod to Hermes himself: his
winged sandals, his errands as herald of Olympus, his journeys to the
Underworld, and his standing as the god of thieves.

Readability comes first. Archaic words are kept to a few that recur,
such as thy and thou, the task list is called the scroll throughout,
and the warnings that data may be lost are left free of flourishes so
their meaning cannot be missed.

Every reply keeps the same placeholders in the same order, so only the
wording changes and not what each reply reports.

The text-UI runner finds the end of the banner by the old greeting,
and many text-UI cases and several JUnit tests expect the old wording.
They fail until a later change brings the tests up to date.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Personality'
LogBookTest: cover every task list operation
commitResults.messageBody:
LogBookTest checks only listTasksDueBy, and four of its cases still
expect the reply from before Hermes gained its own voice, so they fail.

Every change to the list passes through LogBook, and its replies are
what the user reads, so a regression in any of them should fail a test
rather than reach a user.

Let's bring the due-by cases up to date and add cases for adding,
marking, unmarking, deleting, listing, sorting, searching and undoing.
They check the full reply for one task and for several, that a bad task
number changes nothing, and that each change reaches the data file.

Undo is checked after a mark in particular. The saved state must hold
copies of the tasks, or marking alters the saved state too and undo
restores nothing.

commitResults.messageTitle: ParserTest: cover every command and input error
commitResults.messageBody:
ParserTest checks five error messages, all of which still expect the
wording from before Hermes gained its own voice, so every case fails.

The parser decides what each line of input means and explains what is
wrong with input it cannot use, so both need checking.

Let's update those cases and add ones for the command each word builds,
task numbers counting from one, the same number written two ways
counting once, and every message for input that is missing, malformed
or contains the storage separator.

Where the value read from the input matters, the command is run against
a LogBook on a throwaway file, since a command does not expose what it
holds.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the task classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests Task, ToDo, Deadline or Event directly. They are only
exercised through LogBook.

These classes decide how a task is displayed, how it is written to the
data file, when it counts as due and where it falls when sorted, so a
mistake in any of them shows up far from its cause.

Let's test marking and unmarking, the display and file formats of each
kind of task, due dates, the sort order across ranks, and that a copy
is independent of the task it came from.

Dates are kept in August, whose short name is the same in every English
locale, so the expected text does not depend on the machine running the
tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for TaskType
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskType maps each letter in the data file to a kind of task and the
number of fields its line holds, and nothing tests that mapping.

A wrong letter or count would make Hermes skip every task of that kind
when loading, so the mapping is worth pinning down.

Let's check each letter, that unknown letters are refused, each field
count, and that every type's letter reads back as that type.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for reading and writing the data file
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests Storage directly, although it is the only class that
touches the data file.

A fault there costs the user their tasks, either by failing to read
them back or by rejecting lines it should accept.

Let's check that a missing file starts an empty list and creates its
folder, that each kind of task survives a save and a reload, that seven
kinds of damaged line are skipped and counted, that the count starts
afresh on the next load, that a failed save is reported, and that the
separator is refused in any field.

Every case uses a folder JUnit creates and removes, so the real data
file is never read or overwritten.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for reading typed dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests DateTimeFormat, which decides which of the many date and
time layouts a user may type are understood.

Each layout is a separate pattern that could stop matching without
anyone noticing until a user's date is refused.

Let's check that every date-only layout reads as the start of the day,
that every date-and-time layout reads with its time, that text which is
not a date is refused with its wording quoted, and that the format the
refusal suggests is itself accepted.

The twelve-hour layouts are left out. Whether "pm" or "PM" is accepted
depends on the locale of the machine, so such a case would pass on one
machine and fail on another.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for command keywords
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests Keyword, which recognises the command word and holds the
example quoted when input is wrong.

An example that is not itself a valid command would send a user from
one error straight into another.

Let's check that each command word is recognised, that other words and
different capitalisation are not, and that every keyword's example
parses without error.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the commands
commitResults.messageBody:
None of the command classes is tested.

A command is what the parser hands over to be carried out, so one wired
to the wrong operation would do the wrong thing for every user who
types it.

Let's check that each command carries out its change or query, that
errors from LogBook reach the caller, and that only bye ends the
conversation.

The replies themselves are tested in LogBookTest, so these cases check
the effect rather than restating every message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the replies Hermes gives the window
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests Hermes.getResponse or describeSkippedLines, which the
window relies on for every reply and for the warning shown at start-up.

The window colours a reply red and closes when the conversation ends
according to the flags getResponse returns, so a wrong flag changes
what users see.

Let's check that ordinary replies carry neither flag, that bye is
flagged as the end, that input which cannot be parsed or carried out is
flagged as an error, that an unknown word is not, that state carries
between lines, and that the start-up warning counts unreadable lines.

The no-argument constructor and main are left untested because both use
the real data file, which a test must never touch.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for the console
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing tests Ui, which frames every console reply, reads each line the
user types, and words the warning about unreadable records.

The console is one of the two ways users reach Hermes, so what it shows
and how it reads input deserve the same checks as the window's replies.

Let's check that replies and errors are trimmed and framed by dividers,
that the welcome shows the greeting, that typed lines are read in order
without surrounding spaces, and that the warning speaks correctly of one
line or several.

Ui talks to System.in and System.out directly, so each case swaps them
for in-memory streams and puts the real ones back afterwards.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the text-UI tests in favour of JUnit
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has two test suites: a Python script that feeds commands to
Hermes and compares its console output with a plan of expected text,
and the JUnit tests run by gradlew check.

The JUnit tests now cover nearly all of the code that can be tested
automatically, while the text-UI suite has gone stale. Its expected
output and the greeting it looks for still date from before Hermes
gained its own voice, and the CI workflow never ran it.

Let's remove the script, its plan, and the test-ui skill that ran them.
AGENTS.md no longer asks for the plan to be updated and the skill
invoked after a change to what Hermes prints. It asks instead for JUnit
tests covering the change and for gradlew check to pass.

Keeping one suite means there is one place to update when behaviour
changes, and it is the suite CI already runs.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreTesting'
Refuse dates that do not exist
commitResults.messageBody:
A date whose day is past the end of its month is quietly moved to the
last real day of that month. Asking for 30 February stores 28 February,
and the reply shows the changed date rather than refusing the input.

A user who mistypes a day has no way of noticing. Hermes answers as
though it understood, and the task falls due on a day they never named.

Let's resolve dates strictly, so a day that does not exist matches no
format and is refused by the same message as any other unreadable date.

Strict resolving needs uuuu in place of yyyy in every pattern. The yyyy
pattern means the year within an era, which strict resolving will not
accept unless the era is given too, so every date would otherwise be
refused.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say when a parameter is given more than once
commitResults.messageBody:
A command that names /by, /from or /to twice is read as though the
second one were part of the value beside it. Only the first occurrence
separates the parts, so "deadline essay /by A /by B" is reported as the
unreadable date "A /by B".

The complaint sends the user to look at the date, which is the one part
they wrote correctly, and says nothing about the repetition that caused
it.

Let's count each parameter before splitting the arguments and refuse
those given more than once, naming the parameter that was repeated.

The count uses the same pattern the split uses, so a parameter is
counted wherever it would have been treated as a separator.

commitResults.messageTitle: Refuse an event that does not end after it begins
commitResults.messageBody:
An event is accepted whatever its two times are, so one that ends
before it starts is recorded and listed as though it were ordinary.

Such an event cannot happen. It comes of mistyping one of the two
times, and once saved it also sorts by a start the user did not mean.

Let's refuse an end that is not later than the start, quoting both
times as they were typed so the user can see which one is wrong.

An end at the very moment of the start is refused as well. An event of
no length is far more likely a mistyped time than something meant.

The check sits with the parser, where the user's own words are still
at hand. Tasks read from the data file are not checked again, since
refusing them there would quietly drop tasks a user already has.

commitResults.messageTitle: Warn when a task repeats one already listed
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding a task identical to one already on the list is confirmed like
any other, with nothing to say the list now holds it twice.

Two entries that read the same cannot be told apart afterwards. A user
who did not notice cannot say which of them delete 2 would remove, and
one may sit there finished while the other never is.

Let's say so when the new task matches one already listed, as a line
above the usual confirmation.

The task is still added. Repeating an errand may well be meant, and the
user is better placed to judge that than Hermes is, so the warning
leaves the choice to them: undo removes it if it was a mistake.

Tasks are compared by their stored line with the completion flag left
out. That line already holds the kind, description and dates, so the
comparison cannot miss a field the way naming each one could, and a
finished copy still counts as the same errand.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreErrorHandling'
MainWindow: let the mouse wheel scroll the chat
commitResults.messageBody:
The scroll position of the chat area is bound to the height of the
container holding the messages.

That position is a fraction between 0 and 1, so binding it to a height
in pixels sets it to a value in the hundreds. JavaFX clamps neither the
scroll position nor the scroll bar value, so the scroll bar sits far
above its maximum, and each turn of the wheel moves it by a fraction of
one. The wheel therefore appears dead until the user clicks the scroll
bar track, which does clamp the value back into range.

Let's set the scroll position from a listener on that height instead of
binding to it.

A listener keeps the newest message in view, as the binding did, while
leaving the value within range and free for the control to change. The
binding also blocked the control from recording where the view had been
scrolled to, since JavaFX skips that update on a bound property.

commitResults.messageTitle: Suggest numeric dates in every example shown
commitResults.messageBody:
The examples shown when input cannot be read, both the one for a
malformed date and the ones for a malformed deadline, event or due
command, write the month as a name: "27 Aug 2026 1500".

Month names invite the user to type one of their own, and which
abbreviation is accepted depends on the locale of the machine. On an
en_SG machine "Sept" is read and "Sep" is refused, while the reverse
holds elsewhere, so these examples lead users towards input that may
well be rejected.

Let's write every suggested date in the numeric form, as in
"17/08/2026 1500".

An all numeric date carries no such trap, and the day-month-year order
with slashes is the one most readers here will reach for anyway. The
tests that check each suggested example can itself be read are updated
to match, so no message can drift away from what the parser accepts.

commitResults.messageTitle: Correct and tidy the header comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Several header comments do not say what the code they sit above does. MainWindow is headed "Main Window", the check on a task number is headed "Checks to ensure that the index inputted into the method is a valid one", and the guard in delete claims the tasks are being unmarked. Some describe a method by how it is used, as a "helper function", rather than by what it returns. Closing punctuation on tag descriptions is present in some places and missing in others, and two paragraph tags are written as

. Comments that name the wrong operation cost a reader more than no comment at all, and the coding standard asks for a summary that begins with a verb in the third person, for punctuation after each tag description, and for lower case HTML tags. Let's reword the comments that misdescribe their code, drop the one in delete that repeats its own header, and settle the punctuation and tag casing throughout. The guard in delete loses its comment rather than gaining a corrected one because the header comment directly above it already explains, at greater length, why every number is checked before any task is removed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the fields of a stored line
commitResults.messageBody:
Reading a line from the data file indexes into it with bare numbers:
taskParts[2] for the description, [3] and [4] for the dates, and [1]
for the flag saying whether the task is done. The window's smallest
size is written the same way, as 220 and 417 at the point of use.

A reader must count the fields of a stored line to learn what any of
those numbers mean, and a change to the stored format would have to
find every one of them. The comparison against "0" and "1" gives no
hint that these are the two states of a single field.

Let's give each position and each flag a name, and do the same for the
two window measurements.

The names are kept in the class that owns the format, so the meaning of
a field is stated once where the line is read and written, rather than
repeated as a number at each use.

commitResults.messageTitle: LogBook: write marking and unmarking once
commitResults.messageBody:
Marking and unmarking a task are two methods of forty-four lines that
differ in two things: which method of Task they call, and the wording
of the reply. Everything else, from checking the numbers to grouping
the tasks and joining the two halves of the answer, is written twice.

Any change to how a change of completion is reported must be made in
both places, and the day one of them is forgotten the two commands will
answer differently for no reason a reader can see.

Let's write the work once, in a method told which way it is changing
the tasks.

A boolean parameter is preferred over anything more elaborate because
the whole operation then reads from top to bottom in one place, which
matters more here than sparing the reader two short conditionals.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name who the user is talking to above the chat
commitResults.messageBody:
The window opens straight into the conversation. Nothing on screen
says which program is running or that it is listening, and the
greeting scrolls away as soon as a few tasks are added.

A chat with no heading gives a new user nothing to look at while they
work out what to type, and the picture beside each reply is the only
hint of who is answering.

Let's put a bar across the top holding the picture, the name Hermes,
and a line reading online, in the manner of the messaging apps this
window already resembles.

The picture wears the same grey ring as the pictures in the
conversation, and is filled by the same cropping used there, so the
bar looks like part of the same window rather than a panel borrowed
from elsewhere.

The container holding the messages loses the fixed height it was given
by the template. The bar takes 56 pixels from the view, which left that
height taller than what remained and pushed the greeting half out of
sight. Letting the container size itself to the messages it holds is
what it should have done from the start.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show dates the way the user is asked to write them
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are printed with the month as a name, as in "27 Aug 2026 1500",
while every example now asks the user to write a date in figures.

Which abbreviation a month is given depends on the locale of the
machine, so the same task reads "Sept" here and "Sep" elsewhere, and
only one of the two is accepted as input. A user who copies a date out
of the list and types it back may therefore be refused it.

Let's print dates in the same numeric form the examples ask for.

The stored format is left alone: the file still holds an ISO date, so
scrolls written before this change are read back unchanged. Only what
is shown to the user moves, and the tests that quote a printed task
move with it. The tests that feed a month name as input keep it, since
such input is still understood.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set the OS title bar to Hermes
Add a user guide and a product screentshot
commitResults.messageBody:
A reader arricing from the release page will not know how to start
the Hermes application or how to use the commands.

Let's add a screenshot of the running window to showcase to
users the potential of Hermes as well as a user guide to
teach users how to download, navigate the GUI and what the commands
are.

The contents of the guide are organised such that users can get the
high level understanding first and zoom into the specific commands,
features and things to take note of further down the guide. The addition
of a content page further improves the navigability of the user guide,
especially for seasoned users.

Every reply quoted in the guide is copied from a run of the program
rather than written by hand, so no example can claim an answer Hermes
would not give.
